record.original_question: A positive integer is called a pseudo-cube of third kind if some nontrivial permutation of its decimal digits is a perfect cube. Among those numbers, are there infinitely many that are themselves perfect cubes?

evidence.quote: Question: How many pseudo-cubes of third kind are cubes? (We conjecture: an infinity).

artifact.self_contained_problem: Call a positive integer $n$ a "pseudo-cube of the third kind" if there exists a nontrivial permutation of the decimal digits of $n$ (i.e., a permutation different from the identity, and producing a representation without leading zero) that yields a perfect cube. Determine whether there exist infinitely many positive integers $n$ that are themselves perfect cubes and are pseudo-cubes of the third kind; equivalently, prove or disprove that there are infinitely many perfect cubes $m^3$ such that some nontrivial permutation of the decimal digits of $m^3$ is also a perfect cube.
artifact.status_search_result: No published resolution of this question was located. The problem is posed as a conjecture (expecting infinitely many such cubes), and no proof or disproof appears in the available literature. Status remains open to the best of available evidence.

status_evidence.title: Cubic permutations / digit-permutation cubes (general background)
status_evidence.snippet: Cubic permutations are cubes made up of the same digits (e.g., 5027^3 and 7061^3 are digit permutations of one another), but no general result is known on whether infinitely many cubes have nontrivial digit-permutations that are also cubes.
status_evidence.claim: No general theorem is known classifying or producing infinitely many perfect cubes whose digits can be nontrivially permuted to form another perfect cube.
